summary:
Our project is an interactive Martian Resource and Survival Map designed to support future astronauts in exploring Mars and planning safer, more sustainable missions. Covering three important regions—Utopia Planitia, Jezero Crater and Arcadia Planitia—the platform brings together scientific information from multiple Mars exploration missions into one integrated interface.

It combines map layers such as optical imagery, topography, geology, thermal observations, mineralogical evidence and available subsurface water-ice data. By visualizing potential resources, terrain characteristics and scientifically interesting locations, the platform helps explorers investigate where essential materials, particularly water ice, may be found.

The website aims to support Marswalk planning, resource assessment and informed exploration decisions, while reducing dependence on supplies transported from Earth. By making complex planetary data easier to explore and understand, our project takes a step towards safer and more sustainable human exploration of Mars.
details:
What it is. How it works:

AresNav is a web application that looks like Google Maps. It helps plan Marswalks, also known as EVAs on the surface of Mars. AresNav uses science data from NASA. Users can move the map of Utopia Planitia, zoom in and out and switch between a view that shows elevation with shading and a view that shows slope. Users can also add layers that show craters, hazard shading and maps of subsurface water ice. In Plan mode users place a Hab base add science waypoints and set a return point. AresNav then draws the route on the map. The route is coloured by hazard level. AresNav reports the distance, the estimated EVA time the elevation gain and loss the steepest slope, the hazardous distance the number of crater crossings and an elevation profile. A telemetry sidebar shows the elevation, slope, ice consistency and an estimated surface temperature for each inspected location. A time-of-sol slider lets users see temperatures at times of the Martian day. A resource finder ranks the sites for water ice, hydrated clays, hydrated silica and basalt. AresNav also warns about perchlorate in the soil. A region switcher lets users compare areas.

Benefits and intended impact

Mission planners and astronauts can look at candidate sites and routes in one place of dealing with many separate data sets. The goal of AresNav is to make decisions that follow water faster and clearer. AresNav also shows how open NASA data can help resource‑aware EVA planning.

Tools and technology

- Python 3 with NumPy and rasterio/GDAL for data processing

- HTML5 Canvas, plain JavaScript and CSS with no frameworks

- Data: USGS MOLA‑HRSC blended DEM (200 m) SWIM 2.0 ice‑consistency maps and the Robbins & Hynek crater database

- Tested in a desktop browser on a laptop with no special hardware

- AI assistance: Claude from Anthropic helped write and test code

Creativity

AresNav mixes real orbital data with a familiar navigation interface that is built around astronaut decisions. AresNav labels every layer honestly as data‑derived, estimate or unmapped. For example perchlorate appears as a warning of a false map. The single real mineral detection from the Zhurong rover is marked separately.

Factors considered

- Data quality: Data provenance and licensing were checked. The 200 m resolution means hazards are regional‑scale and small boulders may be missed.

- Honest estimates: The temperature model is based on lander measurements. Ice values show consistency, not ice amount.

- Usability: Running without a server or internet makes it easy to demo.

- Status: AresNav is a prototype and not, for operations.
